OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), who is a citizen of Ethiopia and attained permanent residency in Italy. In a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated March 29, 2021, his claim was rejected on grounds that he is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.1 The Appellant provided new evidence, which I have rejected, and thus unable to hold an oral hearing as requested. I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence concerned, including the entire Appellant's Record and written transcript of the RPD hearing. I find the RPD did not err in determining that the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention and that in accordance with section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.2
DETERMINATION

[2] Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA,3 I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.
RPD FINDINGS

[3] The RPD found that the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he had status which is substantially similar to that enjoyed by nationals of Italy at the time of the RPD hearing and that he had not made any allegations against Italy under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA.4
APPELLANT'S ARGUMENTS

[4] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its exclusion analysis.
NEW EVIDENCE

[5] The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected.

[6] The Appellant sought to enter the following as new evidence for this appeal: Expert opinion by XXXX XXXX, Attorney at the Italian Supreme Court and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, Immigration law expert, of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2021.

[7] According to the Law,5 I can only accept evidence that:
i. arose after the RPD Decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

[8] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.6

[9] Appellant's Counsel explains that the new evidence meets the test for admissibility as the Appellant was unable to obtain the evidence before the hearing due to COVID-19 restrictions and due to the limitations of his spouse who resides in Italy. The Appellant explains in his affidavit that he tried to obtain this new evidence when his case was scheduled for a hearing but was unable to retain counsel in Italy at the time. He then states that his spouse tried to retain a firm to provide an expert opinion but was unable to do so because law offices were closed due to COVID-19. Further, he states that he tried to retain a firm online, but firms asked that he or his representative in Italy must communicate with them. This was not possible as his wife, who is in Italy, is not educated and could not use the internet to retain law firms on his behalf. As such, after the easing of COVID-19 restrictions, the Appellant's spouse was able to attend the law firm and retain their services.

[10] I find that this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellant to seek and present to the RPD for his hearing. If the Appellant had made efforts to obtain such evidence prior to his hearing but faced barriers, as explained in his affidavit for this appeal, then it was open to him or his Counsel to explain this to the RPD and request further time to submit such evidence. I have reviewed the transcript and find no mention of the Appellant or his Counsel having sought such evidence for purposes of his RPD hearing. Further, I observe that the Appellant made his refugee claim in August of 2018, was assisted by an Immigration Consultant at that time, and had ample opportunity to collect all documentation in support of his claim prior to restrictions of COVID-19. The Appellant was represented by the same Immigration Consultant at his RPD hearing. As well, I do not find it credible that COVID-19 restrictions were so restrictive that the Appellant would have been unable to communicate with an Italian law firm by phone or other means prior to his RPD hearing for purposes of providing the opinion that is now forwarded for my consideration as new evidence.

[11] For all of these reasons, I find that the new evidence did not arise after the RPD Decision, that it was reasonably available to present to the RPD, and given the significant length of time he had spent in Italy, that evidence related to exclusion would be evidence that the Appellant reasonably would been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD. As I have accepted no new evidence, I am unable to hold an oral hearing.

[16] The Federal Court of Appeal has set out the following three-part test in Zeng:
1. Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded.
2. If the answer is no, the second question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer to the second question is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E.
3. However, if the answer to the second question is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors including, but not limited to: the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary); whether the claimant could return to the third country; the risk the claimant would face in the home country; Canada's international obligations; and any other relevant facts.11

[17] I find that the answer to the first question is "yes" and, as per the JG, I find that the Appellant would be safe in Italy, his country of residence. I note that the Appellant has made no allegations that he faces risk in Italy. As such, the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E.

His wife and two children returned to Italy in 2018 and were living there at the time of the Appellant's RPD hearing. The Appellant testified that his wife and children had permanent residence status in Italy based on his status in Italy. Given this evidence, and the fact that the Appellant is a holder of Italian permanent residency, I find that permanent residents of Italy such as the Appellant enjoy substantially the same rights and responsibility as Italian citizens.

[35] I have also considered additional evidence which I find tips the scale in favour of interpreting the permanent residency policy as discretionary and against an interpretation that there is an automatic loss of permanent residency status and the denial of re-entry for the Appellant to Italian soil. The Appellant is arguing that he lost his permanent residency status because he was absent from Italy for many years and no longer meets one of the conditions for securing permanent residency as he does not have employment in Italy. However, in this case, there is relevant evidence relating to the circumstances of the Appellant's wife and children. His wife and children, who possess Italian permanent residency based on the Appellant's Italian permanent residency status, were able to return to Italy following a long absence from the country without difficulty in 2018. There is no evidence before me that the Appellant's wife had secured employment in Italy, which the Appellant argues is a necessary condition for re-entry to Italy and permanent residency status, when she returned in Italy. I note that when asked by the RPD if his wife was working in Italy his testimony that she was not and was being supported in a house for refugees.24 When asked by his Counsel at the RPD why his wife was allowed to return to Italy in 2018 the Appellant testified that, "Well, basically, the Italians are very flexible for children and for mothers. If they come under any circumstance they will allow them."25 Thus, when I consider the evidence and circumstances related to the Appellant's wife and children who were able to return to Italy without difficulty, I find that this weighs against a finding that permanent residency is lost if one is absent from the country for longer than one year or due to unemployment. Finally, I considered that it was within the Appellant's means to consult Italian authorities before his RPD hearing to determine how he would be treated if he attempted to re-enter Italy or to confirm whether his permanent residency permit in Italy had been revoked, but did not so. I find it is speculative, under the circumstances of a discretionary policy and his wife and children's recent re-entry to Italy with the same permanent resident status without difficulties, that the Appellant would be refused entry at the Italian border while he is possession of a valid permanent residency permit due to his lack of employment and absence from Italy.

[36] The final argument on appeal is that the RPD erred when it dismissed the Appellant's attempted to return to Italy in XXXX 2018 as disingenuous. The RPD found credibility concerns with the Appellant's alleged return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 including his testimony which was noted to provide several disparate answers as to why he was not allowed to enter Italy at that time, that his testimony was incoherent, evolving in nature and that he added details to his story as the hearing progressed. As such, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not genuine in his efforts in XXXX 2018 to return to Italy as a permanent resident.

[38] Furthermore, for reasons which are outlined by the RPD from paragraphs 28 through 38, the RPD found that the Appellant's alleged efforts to return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 were to bolster his allegations that he would not be allowed to enter Italy as a permanent resident at the time of his RPD hearing and that this finding detracted from the Appellant's credibility. Absent any specific argument as to how the RPD erred in arriving at this adverse credibility finding and following my own independent assessment, I see no error which justifies my intervention. Nevertheless, I will elaborate further.

[39] I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony regarding why he was not allowed to enter Italy was disparate and evolving in nature and adopt the RPD's reasons at paragraph 28 as my own. Furthermore, I find that the RPD was correct to disbelieve the Appellant's explanation that he was denied entry to Italy in XXXX 2018 because he had told the authorities in 2014 that he would not be returning to Italy, or for any of the other alleged reasons. At the RPD, the Appellant was asked by his Counsel, "So what happened to you in 2018 when you tried to return to Italy?" to which the Appellant testified, "They said that, told me that you cannot enter because you said when you, before you left that you are not returning. That's why we don't give you access, we don't allow you. That's what they told me."26 When asked what was said to him when he presented himself to Italian immigration, the Appellant testified, "Well, we don't accept you. You used to live here before and when you left, you said that you will not return."27 I find it unlikely that Italian authorities would respond in this way.

[40] Another example of the Appellant's evolving testimony relates to the reasons why he reportedly travelled to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 when he was in possession of a valid Canadian visa issued months earlier. The Appellant in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative, states, "We wanted to try Italy first since we have lived there for some time. Unfortunately, I was told to leave Italy within three days."28 However, when asked by the RPD what the Appellant's intention was when he returned to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, he testified that his intention was to stay for three or four months and then go to Canada as he had a visa.29 At a later point in the hearing, the RPD asked what the purpose was in visiting Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 and the Appellant's testimony was as follows: "Well, I just went to see the situation and come, that was my intention, just to see the situation there and come here."30

[41] I would add that while I am not making a specific credibility finding, that there exist additional reasons for doubting the credibility of the Appellant's account of being refused entry to Italy and these include what the RPD noted to be omissions from his BOC form narrative. For example, the Appellant testified that he tried to enter Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 as a refugee but as noted by the RPD, this was not written in his BOC form narrative. When asked why, the Appellant stated, "I don't know, maybe it was a mistake."31 Further, at the RPD the Appellant testified that he was detained at an airport hotel in Italy for three days and was not permitted to leave. When asked by the RPD why these specific details were missing from his BOC form narrative, the Appellant stated, "I might have forgotten or I might have made a mistake."32

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for dismissing the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), who is a citizen of Ethiopia and attained permanent residency in Italy. In a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated March 29, 2021, his claim was rejected on grounds that he is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.1 The Appellant provided new evidence, which I have rejected, and thus unable to hold an oral hearing as requested. I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence concerned, including the entire Appellant's Record and written transcript of the RPD hearing. I find the RPD did not err in determining that the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention and that in accordance with section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.2
DETERMINATION

[2] Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA,3 I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection.
RPD FINDINGS

[3] The RPD found that the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he had status which is substantially similar to that enjoyed by nationals of Italy at the time of the RPD hearing and that he had not made any allegations against Italy under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA.4
APPELLANT'S ARGUMENTS

[4] The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its exclusion analysis.
NEW EVIDENCE
[5] The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected.

[6] The Appellant sought to enter the following as new evidence for this appeal: Expert opinion by XXXX XXXX, Attorney at the Italian Supreme Court and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, Immigration law expert, of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2021.

[7] According to the Law,5 I can only accept evidence that:
i. arose after the RPD Decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
[8] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.6

[9] Appellant's Counsel explains that the new evidence meets the test for admissibility as the Appellant was unable to obtain the evidence before the hearing due to COVID-19 restrictions and due to the limitations of his spouse who resides in Italy. The Appellant explains in his affidavit that he tried to obtain this new evidence when his case was scheduled for a hearing but was unable to retain counsel in Italy at the time. He then states that his spouse tried to retain a firm to provide an expert opinion but was unable to do so because law offices were closed due to COVID-19. Further, he states that he tried to retain a firm online, but firms asked that he or his representative in Italy must communicate with them. This was not possible as his wife, who is in Italy, is not educated and could not use the internet to retain law firms on his behalf. As such, after the easing of COVID-19 restrictions, the Appellant's spouse was able to attend the law firm and retain their services.

[10] I find that this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellant to seek and present to the RPD for his hearing. If the Appellant had made efforts to obtain such evidence prior to his hearing but faced barriers, as explained in his affidavit for this appeal, then it was open to him or his Counsel to explain this to the RPD and request further time to submit such evidence. I have reviewed the transcript and find no mention of the Appellant or his Counsel having sought such evidence for purposes of his RPD hearing. Further, I observe that the Appellant made his refugee claim in August of 2018, was assisted by an Immigration Consultant at that time, and had ample opportunity to collect all documentation in support of his claim prior to restrictions of COVID-19. The Appellant was represented by the same Immigration Consultant at his RPD hearing. As well, I do not find it credible that COVID-19 restrictions were so restrictive that the Appellant would have been unable to communicate with an Italian law firm by phone or other means prior to his RPD hearing for purposes of providing the opinion that is now forwarded for my consideration as new evidence.

[11] For all of these reasons, I find that the new evidence did not arise after the RPD Decision, that it was reasonably available to present to the RPD, and given the significant length of time he had spent in Italy, that evidence related to exclusion would be evidence that the Appellant reasonably would been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD. As I have accepted no new evidence, I am unable to hold an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS
[12] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.7

[13] The RPD considered and weighed the various pieces of evidence, including the Appellant's own testimony, and ultimately concluded that the Appellant had permanent residence status in Italy and that he had failed to establish that he had lost this status. The RPD considered the factors set out in Shamlou8 and the test articulated in Zeng,9 and found the Appellant has a right to return to Italy, has the right to work and study, and has full access to social services, all of which indicate that the Appellant's permanent residency permit entitled him to status substantially similar to those of nationals of Italy.

[14] The Appellant's arguments centre almost exclusively on the issue of him no longer having permanent residence status in Italy and that the RPD erred in finding that he did. In support of this position, the Appellant relies on objective evidence before the RPD which it is argued proves that he had lost his permanent residence due to being absent from Italy for over 12 months. Further, it
is argued that the RPD erred by dismissing the Appellant's lived experience which clearly establishes that he has lost his status in Italy. Specifically, I am direct to consider the Appellant's experience of being denied entry to Italy in XXXX 2018.

[15] My independent analysis leads me to find that the RPD was correct in their determination that the Appellant should be excluded pursuant to Article 1E from refugee protection. In reaching this decision I have considered the relevant case law and the recently designated Jurisprudential Guide (JG) concerning 1E exclusion.10
Permanent Residence in Italy

[16] The Federal Court of Appeal has set out the following three-part test in Zeng:
1. Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded.
2. If the answer is no, the second question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer to the second question is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E.
3. However, if the answer to the second question is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors including, but not limited to: the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary); whether the claimant could return to the third country; the risk the claimant would face in the home country; Canada's international obligations; and any other relevant facts.11

[17] I find that the answer to the first question is "yes" and, as per the JG, I find that the Appellant would be safe in Italy, his country of residence. I note that the Appellant has made no allegations that he faces risk in Italy. As such, the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E.

[18] Furthermore, the Federal Court in Shamlou has undertaken to assist in determining what is meant by one having status that is "substantially similar" to that of nationals of the country in question, identifying four basic rights that one should enjoy: the right to return to the country of residence; the right to work freely without restriction; the right to study; and full access to social services in the country of residence.12

[19] For the purposes of this appeal, the determinative issue is whether the Appellant possessed permanent residence status in Italy at the time of his RPD hearing.
Rights of Italian Permanent Residents substantially similar to that of Italian Nationals

[20] It is not in dispute that the Appellant, upon his arrival in Canada in XXXX 2018, was in possession of an Italian Permanent Resident card which the Appellant states in his memorandum was first issued in the year 2000.13

[21] The RPD found, based on the available evidence, that the Appellant enjoyed basic rights in respect to being able to return and re-enter Italy, being able to work and study, and accessing social services, that were substantially similar to nationals of Italy.

[22] The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in making this finding, but their argument focuses on the RPD's error in relation to the Appellant's permanent residence status at the time of hearing. I will address this issue below. Overall, I was unable to discern specific argument as to how the RPD erred in its assessment of the relevant factors.

[23] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred when it induced him to speculate on the possibility of his admission to Italy if he accompanied his family and then impugned his credibility. I see no such error committed by the RPD, as the record clearly shows that it was Appellant's Counsel who engaged in the speculation to which the RPD properly objected to. The following from the RPD transcript at page 13 is relevant:14
COUNSEL: Do you think if you had gone to Italy in 2018 with the two children, with your children to Italy, do you think they would have allowed you to enter Italy?
CLAIMANT: I am assuming that they might allow me since I had kids.
COUNSEL: And kids were born in Italy, right?
CLAIMANT: Yes.
COUNSEL: Could that be the reason why your wife was allowed to enter?
RPD MEMBER: Yeah, that's speculation, counsel.
COUNSEL: Yes, it is speculation. I would go with madam member, yes. It is being withdrawn.
MEMBER: Because he would have no idea.

[24] As noted, I was unable to discern specific argument as to how the RPD erred in its assessment of the relevant factors set out in Shamlou15 and my own independent assessment finds no error on the part of the RPD that would justify my intervention. However, I will elaborate.

[25] According to the National Documentation Package (NDP) documentation for Italy, permanent resident permit holders are "...entitled to enter Italy without a visa, to work, to have access to social benefits and services provided by the Italian government and to 'participate in local public life' [footnote omitted]."16 The Appellant testified to having resided in Italy for twenty years, to have been employed in various occupations, received medical services, and his two children were born in Italy and attended school there. His wife and two children returned to Italy in 2018 and were living there at the time of the Appellant's RPD hearing. The Appellant testified that his wife and children had permanent residence status in Italy based on his status in Italy. Given this evidence, and the fact that the Appellant is a holder of Italian permanent residency, I find that permanent residents of Italy such as the Appellant enjoy substantially the same rights and responsibility as Italian citizens.

[26] The point of contention in this appeal is whether, by virtue of his absence from Italy for over 12 months and his lack of employment in Italy, the Appellant still had permanent resident status at the time of his RPD hearing and, therefore, the right to return and exercise the rights associated with that status in Italy.
The Appellant has not lost his status in Italy as a Permanent Resident

[27] The RPD found that the Appellant's Permanent Residency had not expired, and he had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he had lost his status as a permanent resident of Italy, and could return there. In arriving at this conclusion, the RPD considered the objective country documentation which indicated that the permit in possession by the Appellant was a permanent document which did not expire and was valid for an indefinite period of time. Further, the RPD considered that the Appellant had no difficulty renewing his status in Italy for a period of twenty years, that his wife and children had returned to Italy with permanent residency permits, that his wife and children were living in Italy with status as of the day of the RPD hearing, and that their status had been based on the Appellant's status as a permanent resident of Italy.

[28] On appeal it is submitted that the RPD erred and he has no status in Italy. He submits that he has no status by virtue of his absence from Italy for over 12 months, lack of employment in Italy and his recent refusal to enter Italy confirms that he has no status.

[29] I begin my analysis by noting that at the time of the Appellant's RPD hearing, the NDP for Italy contained information about persons granted permanent residency, the entitlements such permanent residency confers on holders, and the conditions that had to be met to acquire this status. To be granted permanent residence, applicants have to have resided in Italy for five years, have sufficient income to support themselves and their dependents, have adequate housing, and pass a language test.17 The Appellant met these conditions as he acquired permanent residency in Italy in 2000 and this is not contested on appeal.

[30] The NDP documentation indicates that permanent residence permit holders are "...entitled to enter Italy without a visa, to work, to have access to social benefits and services provided by the Italian government and to 'participate in local public life' [footnote omitted]."18

[31] The RPD correctly found that the Appellant's Italian permanent residency permit has no expiry date.19 Item 3.7 in the NDP for Italy describes the permanent residency permit as permanent and to never expire. Further, it is noted that while the bearer is required to update the photograph every five years and revalidate the permit every ten years by submitting a copy of the permit, passport and residence/family status that, even if the photograph is not updated, the permit expires as a valid identification tool but "never as a vested right."20

[32] The Appellant has directed me to consider information in the country documentation for Italy, item 3.8, and specifically the information about reacquiring permanent resident status. However, I
find that the evidence is insufficient to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's Italian permanent residency has in fact been revoked for reasons which are said to be his absence from Italy for more than 12 months and lack of employment in Italy.

[33] I note that at the outset of item 3.8, according to the website of the Italian General Directorate of Immigration and Integration Policies, it states "[t]he EU long-term residence permit may [my emphasis] be revoked in the following cases: an expulsion measure has been adopted against the foreign national; the permit was acquired fraudulently; the individual is considered dangerous with relevance to the public order and security; the foreign national no longer fulfills the requirements set for its issue; absence from the territory of the [EU] for a period of 12 consecutive months; acquisition of a long-term resident status in another [EU] member State; and absence from Italy for a period exceeding six years."21 This information was confirmed by an individual from the same agency. I find that the use of the word "may" means the loss is not automatic.

[34] I find that the Italian policy on permanent residency permits and the rights enjoyed by their holders, includes only the language that revocation of the rights associated with the permanent residency cards may be revoked if one of a number of conditions exist. Further, I note that even in the event of a loss of permanent residence, this is not the final decision and one can appeal or challenge the decision through legal channels.22 Overall, I find that the documentation in the NDP for Italy are insufficient to find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant has lost his status as a permanent resident of Italy as alleged, or that he would have no recourse to have it renewed or reinstated in his situation and circumstances. I am mindful of the evidence and case law, which supports the finding that, where revocation of status is discretionary or not automatic, it is not an error to find that the right of return exists.23

[35] I have also considered additional evidence which I find tips the scale in favour of interpreting the permanent residency policy as discretionary and against an interpretation that there is an automatic loss of permanent residency status and the denial of re-entry for the Appellant to Italian soil. The Appellant is arguing that he lost his permanent residency status because he was absent from Italy for many years and no longer meets one of the conditions for securing permanent residency as he does not have employment in Italy. However, in this case, there is relevant evidence relating to the circumstances of the Appellant's wife and children. His wife and children, who possess Italian permanent residency based on the Appellant's Italian permanent residency status, were able to return to Italy following a long absence from the country without difficulty in 2018. There is no evidence before me that the Appellant's wife had secured employment in Italy, which the Appellant argues is a necessary condition for re-entry to Italy and permanent residency status, when she returned in Italy. I note that when asked by the RPD if his wife was working in Italy his testimony that she was not and was being supported in a house for refugees.24 When asked by his Counsel at the RPD why his wife was allowed to return to Italy in 2018 the Appellant testified that, "Well, basically, the Italians are very flexible for children and for mothers. If they come under any circumstance they will allow them."25 Thus, when I consider the evidence and circumstances related to the Appellant's wife and children who were able to return to Italy without difficulty, I find that this weighs against a finding that permanent residency is lost if one is absent from the country for longer than one year or due to unemployment. Finally, I considered that it was within the Appellant's means to consult Italian authorities before his RPD hearing to determine how he would be treated if he attempted to re-enter Italy or to confirm whether his permanent residency permit in Italy had been revoked, but did not so. I find it is speculative, under the circumstances of a discretionary policy and his wife and children's recent re-entry to Italy with the same permanent resident status without difficulties, that the Appellant would be refused entry at the Italian border while he is possession of a valid permanent residency permit due to his lack of employment and absence from Italy.

[36] The final argument on appeal is that the RPD erred when it dismissed the Appellant's attempted to return to Italy in XXXX 2018 as disingenuous. I note that there are no specific reasons outlined as to how specifically the RPD erred in finding that there were credibility issues with the Appellant's evidence regarding his attempted return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018.

[37] The Appellant, in support of his allegation that he had no status in Italy and cannot return as a permanent resident, alleged that he attempted to return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 as a permanent resident but was not allowed to enter Italy. The RPD found credibility concerns with the Appellant's alleged return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 including his testimony which was noted to provide several disparate answers as to why he was not allowed to enter Italy at that time, that his testimony was incoherent, evolving in nature and that he added details to his story as the hearing progressed. As such, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not genuine in his efforts in XXXX 2018 to return to Italy as a permanent resident.

[38] Furthermore, for reasons which are outlined by the RPD from paragraphs 28 through 38, the RPD found that the Appellant's alleged efforts to return to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 were to bolster his allegations that he would not be allowed to enter Italy as a permanent resident at the time of his RPD hearing and that this finding detracted from the Appellant's credibility. Absent any specific argument as to how the RPD erred in arriving at this adverse credibility finding and following my own independent assessment, I see no error which justifies my intervention. Nevertheless, I will elaborate further.

[39] I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony regarding why he was not allowed to enter Italy was disparate and evolving in nature and adopt the RPD's reasons at paragraph 28 as my own. Furthermore, I find that the RPD was correct to disbelieve the Appellant's explanation that he was denied entry to Italy in XXXX 2018 because he had told the authorities in 2014 that he would not be returning to Italy, or for any of the other alleged reasons. At the RPD, the Appellant was asked by his Counsel, "So what happened to you in 2018 when you tried to return to Italy?" to which the Appellant testified, "They said that, told me that you cannot enter because you said when you, before you left that you are not returning. That's why we don't give you access, we don't allow you. That's what they told me."26 When asked what was said to him when he presented himself to Italian immigration, the Appellant testified, "Well, we don't accept you. You used to live here before and when you left, you said that you will not return."27 I find it unlikely that Italian authorities would respond in this way.

[40] Another example of the Appellant's evolving testimony relates to the reasons why he reportedly travelled to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 when he was in possession of a valid Canadian visa issued months earlier. The Appellant in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form narrative, states, "We wanted to try Italy first since we have lived there for some time. Unfortunately, I was told to leave Italy within three days."28 However, when asked by the RPD what the Appellant's intention was when he returned to Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, he testified that his intention was to stay for three or four months and then go to Canada as he had a visa.29 At a later point in the hearing, the RPD asked what the purpose was in visiting Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 and the Appellant's testimony was as follows: "Well, I just went to see the situation and come, that was my intention, just to see the situation there and come here."30

[41] I would add that while I am not making a specific credibility finding, that there exist additional reasons for doubting the credibility of the Appellant's account of being refused entry to Italy and these include what the RPD noted to be omissions from his BOC form narrative. For example, the Appellant testified that he tried to enter Italy on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 as a refugee but as noted by the RPD, this was not written in his BOC form narrative. When asked why, the Appellant stated, "I don't know, maybe it was a mistake."31 Further, at the RPD the Appellant testified that he was detained at an airport hotel in Italy for three days and was not permitted to leave. When asked by the RPD why these specific details were missing from his BOC form narrative, the Appellant stated, "I might have forgotten or I might have made a mistake."32

[42] Based on all of this evidence, I find that the Appellant held valid permanent resident status in Italy and a right to return to Italy on the date of his RPD hearing and thus, my analysis need not address the other factors identified in Zeng. Further, as there is no claim or allegations made that there exists risk of persecution or probability of harm for the Appellant in Italy, there is no need for me to assess risk in Italy.

[43] The RPD was correct to find that the Appellant is excluded under Article 1E of the Convention because he had status which is substantially similar to that enjoyed by nationals of Italy at the time of the RPD hearing.
CONCLUSION

[44] I dismiss the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is excluded pursuant to Article 1E and is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
